An English naturalist who worked out the theory of evolution by natural selection on his own, while collecting animals in the Malay Archipelago, and who mapped the boundary between Asian and Australian wildlife now called the Wallace Line.

Wallace came from a poor family and paid for his travels by selling specimens. After four years in the Amazon, whose collections were lost when his ship burned, he spent eight years, from 1854 to 1862, in the islands of today's Malaysia and Indonesia. He gathered over 100,000 specimens. In 1858, on or near Ternate in the Moluccas, during a fever, he grasped how species change. He sent his essay to Charles Darwin, who had been working on the same idea for twenty years. Their papers were read together in London that July, and Darwin rushed out On the Origin of Species the next year.

Wallace noticed that animals on Bali and Borneo were Asian, while those on Lombok and Sulawesi had Australian links, and drew the line between them: the Wallace Line. His book The Malay Archipelago (1869) is a classic of travel writing. He is seen as a founder of biogeography.
sum: An English naturalist who worked out the theory of evolution by natural selection on his own, while collecting animals in the Malay Archipelago, and who mapped the boundary between Asian and Australian wildlife now called the Wallace Line.
